findings.claim: Every new attribute line sits inside `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0. So consumers compiling for netstandard2.0 or SDK-style .NET Framework get formatters and resolvers with no attribute. That fails the requirement 'All generated code is decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage' for a large share of users, and the guard is not needed for compilation.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageGapTests.GeneratedFormatters_AreDecorated_WhenTargetSymbolDefined. It first proves the attribute type resolves from the netstandard2.0 reference assemblies. It then runs the generator with NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK defined and expects every generated IMessagePackFormatter class to carry the attribute. It fails on head. The same `#if` guard appears in EnumTemplate.tt, UnionTemplate.tt, StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt, ResolverTemplate.tt and CompositeResolverTemplate.tt.

findings.claim: The resolver templates now add `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` to the user's own `partial class` resolver declaration. `ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` has AllowMultiple=false. A user who already put `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on their `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class` (the obvious manual workaround for this very issue) now gets CS0579 'Duplicate attribute', so existing valid code stops compiling. The same applies to the composite resolver template.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageGapTests.UserResolverAlreadyExcludedFromCoverage_StillCompiles. The user resolver partial already carries [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage], and the test asserts the generator output compilation has no errors. It passes on base and fails on head with CS0579. The same applies to CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:8.

findings.claim: The new README text says the attribute is 'only emitted for targets where it is available (not netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework)'. That is factually wrong: the attribute is available on both, so the docs justify the coverage gap with a false premise.

receipt_plan.detail: The first assertion in ExcludeFromCodeCoverageGapTests.GeneratedFormatters_AreDecorated_WhenTargetSymbolDefined resolves ReferenceAssemblies.NetStandard.NetStandard20 and finds System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute via GetTypeByMetadataName. That contradicts the README sentence.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Emit [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] with no setting at all. This is what the change does: each formatter, enum, union, string-key and resolver template, plus the resolver's nested FormatterCache/GetFormatterHelper, writes the attribute (here inside an #if guard), and no option exists to turn it off.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: Emit the attribute by default but add an opt-out setting, which the requirement explicitly calls acceptable. This needs a new bool (for example `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`, default true) on the generator options, read from the existing options attribute or analyzer config. Each template wraps its attribute lines in `<# if (Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage) { #> ... <# } #>`, the .cs transforms are regenerated, README documents the switch, and a snapshot test covers the opted-out output.
